question: Which statement best describes Global CSS?
options: Global CSS can affect many elements across the application. It is useful for resets, base typography, and shared styles. It is like a building-wide rule about lighting. Keep global selectors modest because a broad change can alter unrelated pages. In Next.js, follow the project’s supported place for importing global styles. For example, use global CSS for a small set of app-wide defaults, not page-specific selectors.

CSS variables can store colors, spacing, and other values used across components. A shared token lets a theme change one value instead of many separate rules. It is like a palette card used by the whole design team. Name variables by purpose and ensure contrast remains readable when themes change. For example, use responsive rules when a layout no longer fits, not only at arbitrary device labels.

A CSS Module scopes its class names to a file when imported by a component. This lowers the chance that two components accidentally use the same style name. It is like a label that only applies inside one folder. Modules are useful for component-specific styles that should not leak elsewhere. For example, keep a CSS Module next to a component when its styles should stay local.

Import a CSS Module and use its exported class names on elements. The build system maps them to generated names while preserving the local reference in code. It is like using a local nickname that is translated to a unique label. Keep the module close to its component so changes are easy to locate. For example, share spacing tokens through CSS variables so one design adjustment updates related parts.
